result.summary: Pausanias lists famous cases of treason in Greek history, from the Ionians under Darius to Athens under Antipater. He then explains how Callicrates, after Rome defeated Perseus, denounced Achaeans to a Roman senator, leading to more than 1,000 being sent to Italy and held for seventeen years.

scenes.title: A history of Greek betrayals
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists traitors who ruined Greek cities, from the Ionian revolt to the Macedonian garrisons in Athens.
scenes.stakes: Greek cities lose their freedom through betrayal by their own leading men.

scenes.title: Callicrates accuses the Achaeans
scenes.summary: After Perseus falls, Callicrates wins over a Roman senator, who at an Achaean assembly accuses the leading Achaeans of helping Perseus.
scenes.stakes: Achaean leaders risk death on an unproven charge, and the League risks losing its independence.

scenes.title: Achaeans sent to Rome
scenes.summary: Xeno offers to be tried, and the senator uses this to send the accused to Rome. Over 1,000 are imprisoned in Etruria, and about 300 are freed after seventeen years.
scenes.stakes: The accused Achaeans face imprisonment without trial, and escapees face immediate execution.

characters.name: Xenias
characters.description: Elean who tried to betray Elis

alias_notes.explanation: Pausanias often calls the Persians Medes.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias sums up Greece's recurring weakness for treason.
Marks the unprecedented Roman demand to send accused Greeks abroad for trial.

analysis.text: Pausanias blames Greek downfall on internal betrayal rather than foreign strength, tracing a pattern from the Persian wars to Rome.
The deportation of Achaeans after Pydna (167 BC) shows Rome's growing control over Greece, which ended with the Achaean War and Corinth's destruction in 146 BC.

fun_facts.text: The historian Polybius was among the Achaeans deported to Italy after Pydna and used his stay to study Rome.

language_notes.text: The Ionian revolt against Persia ended at the sea battle of Lade (494 BC), where most Samian ships reportedly deserted. Herodotus tells of this.
The Aleuadæ were the ruling family of Thessaly, who sided with Xerxes' Persian invasion in 480 BC.
The Lamian War (323–322 BC) was the Greek revolt against Macedon after Alexander's death; Antipater was besieged at Lamia before his victory.
"Commonalty" means the common people, the citizen body as opposed to its leaders.
The reverse in Bœotia is the defeat at Chaeronea (338 BC), where Philip beat Athens and Thebes.
Archilochus was a seventh-century BC poet of Paros, famed for iambic verse; Pausanias cites him as the source that mentions the Sapæans (Thracian people).
"By no means remarkable for justice" is understatement: the senator is implied to be unjust and easily corrupted by flattery.
"Confuted" means refuted or proved wrong; the senator, once refuted, simply broadens his accusation instead of retreating.
The Amphictyonic Council was the league of Greek peoples that administered Delphi's sanctuary and judged religious and some inter-state disputes.
"Some 300 or even fewer" is Pausanias hedging about the number of survivors after seventeen years of detention.

context_notes.text: Eretria, on Euboea, was sacked by the Persians in 490 BC, shortly before Marathon, after some of its leading men betrayed it.
Lysander was the Spartan admiral who won the Peloponnesian War in 404 BC and set up pro-Spartan oligarchies in Greek cities.
Demades was an Athenian orator who collaborated with Macedon and later served Antipater.
Perseus was defeated at Pydna in 168 BC; Rome then sent commissioners to organize Macedonia and investigate Greek states' conduct.
Etruria, in central Italy, was Roman-controlled territory; the Achaeans were held as hostages there, among them the historian Polybius, though he is not named here.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias opens with a moral judgment, framing the whole survey of Greek history as a lesson on treason.
Comparing treason's damage to the plague stresses how destructive betrayal was, a vivid and emphatic exaggeration.
Treason is called an "itch," presenting it as a persistent, almost bodily affliction of the Greeks.
The verb "insinuated" and the picture of constant flattery portray Callicrates as a sly, servile opportunist.
Xeno's honest confidence in his innocence is what the senator exploits, so his virtue becomes the cause of the disaster.
Stressing that this was unprecedented signals a grave turning point, the loss of Greek legal independence under Rome.
